I dwell on how I used to be before the event
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a patient whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, sexual-trauma-specific trigger content is a poor fit unless sexual violence was part of the witnessed events. Nothing else in the profile links the trauma memory or threat meanings to sexual content, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Avoiding sex is similarly trauma-content-specific and is not supported by the rest of the trigger, threat, or memory items for witnessed childhood domestic violence. In combination with the sexual-trauma trigger item, it suggests a different trauma theme than the one provided, making the profile clinically incoherent.

vignette:
Karim is a 41-year-old construction worker who came to treatment after years of telling himself that what happened was long ago and should no longer matter. He grew up in an immigrant Middle Eastern family in the United States, and when he speaks about childhood he does so unevenly, as if moving over broken ground. The central event he returns to is not a single argument but a night of domestic violence he witnessed as a boy, when a confrontation between adults in his home escalated beyond anything he could understand or stop. What remains with him is strangely fragmented. He says there are parts he cannot deliberately bring back no matter how hard he tries, as if the memory locks when he reaches for it on purpose. Yet certain images arrive with brutal sharpness, “like photographs,” fixed and flat in his mind: a face tightened with rage, the angle of a body in a doorway, the look in someone’s eyes just before things turned dangerous. Between these snapshots are blanks he cannot fill.

In the years after, Karim learned to read a room before he entered it. He watched faces, shoulders, the set of a jaw, the way someone stood too close or held themselves too stiffly. He became the kind of person who could tell himself he was just observant, but in practice he was scanning constantly for signs that someone might turn threatening. Confrontation came to feel less like an ordinary part of life and more like the edge of something catastrophic. If voices sharpened or two people squared off with each other, his body reacted before he had time to think. He describes his chest tightening, his stomach dropping, heat climbing up his neck, and an electric feeling in his arms as though he needed to brace for impact. Police are especially potent for him. The sight of an officer near a traffic stop, outside a store, or passing by a construction site is enough to make him tense and track every movement around him. The authority in the uniform, the possibility that a conflict is unfolding nearby, and the uncertainty about what might happen all catch at him at once.

Karim works on construction crews where disputes are common enough—someone blaming another trade for delays, a foreman pressing workers on deadlines, a subcontractor arguing over materials. He has become known as quiet and easygoing, but this comes at a cost. If he senses disagreement building, he finds a reason to step away, volunteer for a task at the far end of the site, or keep his head down and say nothing. He does not think of this as passivity. To him it feels prudent, the safest way to prevent things from tipping into danger. Over time, though, it has narrowed his world. He avoids speaking up even when he needs clarification, and when something on the job takes longer than expected—when a supervisor says, “Hang on, I’ll come back,” and doesn’t, or when a delivery is late, or when he is called into the trailer and made to wait—his mind jumps immediately to the sense that something bad is happening. He sits there keyed up, studying footsteps, voices, and expressions, certain there is trouble just out of sight.

Outside work, conversations about the future unsettle him in a way he finds hard to explain. If friends ask where he sees himself in a few years, whether he wants a family, whether he might move up to a steadier role, he feels himself pull away. Future talk carries a kind of exposure for him, as if making plans invites something to go wrong. He often drifts off mentally instead, disappearing into private fantasy and distance while the conversation continues around him. At other times he turns backward, dwelling on who he was before that violent home atmosphere shaped him so thoroughly. He thinks about a version of himself who might have been more open, less guarded, more able to stay present with people. These thoughts are painful but familiar, and he circles them often when he is alone.

What brought him to seek help now was not one dramatic collapse but accumulation. On a recent job, a heated exchange broke out between a foreman and another worker, and Karim felt the now-familiar surge in his body so strongly that he had to leave the area and sit in his truck until he could steady himself. Later that same week, he was called into a meeting and left waiting outside the office; by the time he was invited in, he was convinced someone had been hurt or that he was about to be blamed for something. He has started to see how much of his day is organized around watching, bracing, and sidestepping. He says he is tired of disappearing into his head and tired of living as if every confrontation is the beginning of the worst thing. What frightens him most is that he will stay this way permanently, unable to be around ordinary conflict or to imagine any future without dread. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to remain in the present when something reminds him of the past, and to stop feeling that every face, every delay, every authority figure might signal danger.
